quote: Consistently within and across experiments, all-female groups (a female subject alongside female confederates) conform significantly more often than all-male groups.
content: "Consistently" is too strong, given the author-sex moderator. Eagly and Carli's meta-analysis also found that the sex difference was largest in group-pressure paradigms with surveillance, which is the Asch setup exactly (Eagly & Carli 1981). The essay took the sex effect from Bond & Smith, its cited source, which does report it. The sentence Fable objects to is also not a claim about women. It is a reductio aimed at the hypothesis that conformity is rational. If average behaviour is rational, and the sexes differ reliably in a paradigm with one correct answer, then at least one sex is off the rational policy. That argument needs only a difference, and a small difference will do. The essay never claims the effect is fixed human nature, and the historical decline is an interesting fact that does not bear on its argument.

quote: Paul Crowley reminds me to note that when subjects can respond in a way that will not be seen by the group, conformity also drops, which also argues against an Aumann interpretation.
content: Deutsch & Gerard should have been cited. What the essay adds is a norm, and Deutsch & Gerard did not supply one. They separated informational from normative influence. They did not ask how much informational influence a rational observer should accept, and the Bayesian benchmark is what makes the details diagnostic. Honest observers of the same diagram are evidence, and fifteen of them should count for more than three. Conformity that levels off at three confederates is therefore too small to be informational and too flat to be updating, which is the essay's argument and not one the 1955 paper makes. The essay also asks only for an "intuitive version of Aumann's Agreement": symmetric reliability among observers of the same stimulus, with no common prior over the world required.
